name: Embedded analytics
description: Analytics shipped as product surface: dashboards, reports, and metrics rendered inside your application for your customers, holding to product-grade latency and strict tenant isolation. The stack inverts internal-BI priorities — a fast OLAP store (or warehouse tuned for concurrency) does the scanning, a semantic layer defines metrics once and enforces row-level tenancy and caching in front of every query, and the presentation layer is either an embeddable BI tool (fast to ship, styling limits) or custom components over the semantic layer's API (full control, more build). Tenancy enforcement belongs in the semantic layer or below, never in frontend query-building: a customer seeing another tenant's numbers is a security incident, not a bug.
when_to_use: Choose this when analytics is part of the product's value proposition — usage dashboards in a SaaS app, campaign reporting for advertisers, portfolio views for clients — with real concurrency and sub-second expectations at the 95th percentile.
It fits as soon as ad-hoc, per-customer report exports stop scaling or analytics becomes a priced tier.
Analytics is part of the product's value proposition, not an internal tool.
when_not_to_use: Internal dashboards do not need this — blueprint 2's BI layer serves employees fine at a fraction of the effort.
If only a handful of enterprise customers need reports, scheduled exports or a shared BI folder buys time honestly.
And do not point embedded workloads at the same warehouse compute your analysts use: customer-facing p95 latency and month-end analyst scans are incompatible tenants.

hot_spots.title: Tenant isolation
hot_spots.detail: One missing row-level filter is a cross-customer data breach.

hot_spots.title: Noisy neighbors
hot_spots.detail: A single heavy tenant degrades dashboards for everyone.

hot_spots.title: Semantic drift
hot_spots.detail: In-product metrics diverging from internal BI erodes customer trust.

evolution.reason: Customer-facing dashboards start demanding sub-second freshness.
Add tenant isolation, metering, and a semantic API when embedded dashboards scale to many customers.

stages.name: Landing
stages.role: Immutable raw dump of product data before modeling
stages.rationale: Cheap immutable object storage as the landing layer decouples ingestion from processing: replays, backfills, and audits read the raw dump instead of re-extracting from sources.

stages.name: Warehouse/OLAP
stages.role: Serve customer-facing query volume at product latency and concurrency
stages.rationale: ClickHouse is the workhorse of embedded analytics — millisecond scans, high concurrency for the money, and materialized views that pre-shape per-tenant aggregates; design tables tenant-first (tenant_id leading the sort key) and most latency problems never appear. Pinot overtakes it at very high QPS user-facing workloads where its index arsenal shines; StarRocks when customer dashboards need real joins rather than denormalized tables. Serving straight from Snowflake (dedicated warehouse, aggressive caching) is legitimate at modest concurrency and keeps one platform — until the compute bill says otherwise; DuckDB embedded per-tenant is a clever pattern for small isolated datasets.

stages.name: Semantic layer
stages.role: Define metrics once; enforce row-level tenancy, caching, and a stable API between store and product
stages.rationale: Cube was practically built for this seat: metric definitions as code, security contexts that inject tenant filters into every query from the app's JWT (tenancy enforced below the UI, where it belongs), pre-aggregations that make p95 latency survivable, and REST/GraphQL/SQL APIs that both embeddable BI tools and custom frontends consume. This layer is what keeps 'revenue' identical across the in-app dashboard and the CSV export, and what lets you swap the store later without touching product code. The dbt Semantic Layer keeps definitions beside your models but has a thinner embedded/consumption story; AtScale plays here at enterprise scale. Skipping the layer and hand-writing tenant-filtered SQL in the backend works right up until the second surface ships.

stages.name: Embedded BI
stages.role: Render dashboards inside the product: embeddable open-source BI, or custom components over the semantic API — the doc's 'custom' half is your frontend code
stages.rationale: Superset's embedded SDK with guest tokens is the strongest open-source path to shipping real dashboards in-app quickly — full chart builder, no per-viewer licensing, self-hosted so data stays put; its limits are styling depth and the operational care Superset itself needs. Metabase embedding (interactive or static) is simpler to run and fine for straightforward dashboards, with licensing tiers to watch; Grafana suits ops-flavored embedded views. The custom path — your own React components calling Cube's APIs, with a charting library — costs the most and is where successful analytics products usually end up, because pixel-perfect brand fit and UX control eventually beat any embedded tool; many teams sensibly ship Superset first and migrate surface by surface. Streamlit covers the internal-prototype rung of that ladder.

stages.name: Row-level tenancy
stages.role: Guarantee each customer sees only their rows — an enforcement pattern spanning the semantic layer and store, not a standalone product
stages.rationale: Tenancy is a property you enforce in depth, not a tool you install, hence no recommended slug. The primary control is the semantic layer's security context (Cube injecting tenant_id from a server-verified JWT into every query); back it with store-level defense — ClickHouse row policies, Postgres RLS if serving from Postgres, per-tenant database/schema isolation when contracts demand hard separation — so a bug in one layer is not a breach. OPA fits when tenancy rules are complex enough to centralize as policy. Test it like the security boundary it is: automated cross-tenant leakage tests in CI, and never accept tenant identifiers from the client side of the trust boundary.
